newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Moody's says Argentine banking system still weak.
newsitem.headline: Moody's says Argentine banking system still weak.

text.p: Moody's Investors Corp said Monday that Argentina's banking system continues to be hampered by overall weak financial fundamentals.

Speaking at a banking conference in Buenos Aires, Daniel Sarp, assistant vice president of Moody's, said: "Continued poor loan performance, together with low levels of profitability, have hampered a number of banks' ability to materially reduce non-performing loan portfolios."
On the other hand, Sarp said there are dynamics of change in the Argentine financial sector which include "mainly enchanced competition, consolidations and prospects for growth."
But, increased competition in the system will also "induce key players to tap into riskier segments of the underbanked market, namely the consumer/retail sector," said Sarp.

At the same time, the increased presence of foreign banks in Argentina will "further improve the underwriting standards of Argentine banks and, in certain instances, enhance capitalization levels of banks."
This will lead to improved efficiency of the local banking sector, but only in the long-term, said Sarp.
Turning to the issue of dollarization, Sarp indicated he did not share the recent change in the ratings criteria announced by competitor Standard & Poor's.
Dollarization is the term used to describe an economy where the dollar or another hard currency replaces the local currency as the main store of value.

S&P eased the sovereign rating ceiling on several Argentine corporations and banks because it considers the level of dollarization in Argentina's economy as making it very unlikely the government would interfere with firm's transfers of foreign currency.
That led to the upgrade of several Argentine financial institutions to up to two grades higher than the sovereign.

However, "Moody's bank ratings for bonds and deposits are, by definition, constrained by country ceilings which take into account foreign currency transfer risk and are based upon an assessment of economic and political factors," said Sarp.
S&P implied by its upgrade of the banks that Argentine financial institutions will be able to service foreign currency obligations even if the sovereign may not be able to do so.

But, "convertibility does not mean that the Argentine banks are necessarily sitting on dollars. It means a fixed exchange rate whereupon the government has committed itself to exchange, buy or sell - on demand - dollars at parity," said Sarp.

"Argentina does not create the currency, therefore, there is no guarantee of payment; there is no lender of last resort in Argentina. Given the difficulty in calling dollar loans, if many depositors were to redeem their dollars, a liquidity crisis would occur," added Sarp.
As in 1995 following the crisis induced by the Mexican peso devaluation, in the event of another financial shock Argentina "would depend upon the goodwill of the international community."
During the "Tequila crisis" about 20 percent of the bank deposits in the banking system were withdrawn.
